The Work, Teaching and Scholarly-Scientific Legacy of Rabbi Meir ibn Aldabi: Studies in His Work "Shevilei Emunah"
Historical Context, Biography and Halakhic Lineage
Rabbi Meir ben Yitzhak ibn Aldabi (c. 1310–1360) was active in a central period of transition in the spiritual history of the people of Israel in the 14th century [cite: 1, 2]. His thought represents an intellectual crossroads at which the halakhic tradition of the schools of Ashkenaz and Sepharad, Aristotelian and Maimonidean philosophical inquiry, and early kabbalistic mysticism met, alongside the political science and medicine of the Middle Ages [cite: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
Rabbi Meir was born in the city of Toledo (Toletula) in the region of Andalusia in Spain [cite: 1, 2, 5]. He grew up in a distinguished family, the youngest son of Rabbi Yitzhak ibn Aldabi, who is described in his book as "the pious one", and of the distinguished lineage of "the exiles of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad" [cite: 1, 2]. His principal asset of lineage in the scholarly world was the fact that he was the grandson of the leading halakhic authority of the generation, Rabbi Asher ben Yehiel (the Rosh, c. 1250–1327) [cite: 1, 2, 4, 5]. This family connection is not merely a biographical detail but a fundamental layer of his halakhic authority and of the content of his work [cite: 1].
In his book "Shevilei Emunah", Rabbi Meir incorporates four direct halakhic and practical testimonies from his grandfather the Rosh, consistently calling him "my grandfather the Rosh, of blessed memory" [cite: 1]. These testimonies reflect an unmediated tradition of the study hall [cite: 1]:
1. Laws of family purity and care of the sick: the ruling of the Rosh that the wife of a sick man who is a niddah (menstruant) is permitted to attend to him and care for him, provided that she refrains from washing his face, hands and feet and from making his bed in his presence [cite: 1].
2. Laws of the order of hand-washing and the meal: the personal custom of the Rosh to check himself before the meal whether he needed to relieve himself, to wash his hands and recite the blessing "Asher Yatzar", and afterwards to wash his hands a second time for the meal and recite the blessing "Al Netilat Yadayim" [cite: 1].
3. Laws of breaking the bread: the instruction of the Rosh to cut a little of the bread before the blessing and leave it attached, so that there should be no interruption between the blessing and the eating [cite: 1].
4. Laws of the blessings over drinks: the ruling of the Rosh concerning one who has no wine and is thirsty for water, who drinks a little water before the meal in order to cover the drinking during the meal, and likewise the law concerning one who has food stuck in his throat [cite: 1].
A chronological analysis of their lifetimes shows that Rabbi Meir was born while his grandfather the Rosh was still alive [cite: 1]. In scholarship it is commonly estimated that Rabbi Meir was the son of a daughter or of a son of the Rosh, and belonged to the third generation that saw the great halakhic authority in Spain [cite: 1].
Rabbi Meir's life was not tranquil. In the poetic introduction to his book he describes tribulations, decrees and persecutions that befell him and his family in his country, which uprooted him from his father's house and caused him hard wanderings [cite: 1, 2, 5]. These circumstances led him to leave Spain and go up to the Land of Israel [cite: 1, 2, 4, 5]. Around 1348 he settled in Mamluk Jerusalem, which was then a developing center for kabbalists and thinkers [cite: 1, 2, 4]. In Jerusalem he completed the writing of his great work "Shevilei Emunah" in the year 5120 from the creation of the world (1360 of the common era), in which, as far as is known, he died, at about fifty years of age [cite: 1, 2, 4, 5].
The Structure and Encyclopedic Character of "Shevilei Emunah"
The only book of Rabbi Meir ibn Aldabi that has come down to us is "Shevilei Emunah" ("Paths of Faith") [cite: 1, 5]. The title of the book is derived from the verse "I have chosen the way of faithfulness; Your ordinances have I set before me" (Psalms 119:30), and at the same time the author's name is alluded to by gematria and in an acrostic in the opening poem [cite: 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. The work belongs to the eclectic encyclopedic genre, a genre that was very popular among Jewish thinkers in the Middle Ages and whose aim was to gather under one roof the whole body of religious, scientific, medical and philosophical knowledge needed by the enlightened believer [cite: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7].
The work is built on an architectural framework composed of ten "Paths" (netivim, main chapters), divided into "Trails" (shevilim, subsections) [cite: 2, 4, 5, 7, 10]:
Path | Main subject | Details of the contents and the trails
The First Path | Faith in the Creator and His unity | Contains one trail: the existence of God, His unity, the negation of corporeality, His eternity, and an explanation of the holy names and the sefirot according to the secret of the Kabbalah [cite: 5, 7].
The Second Path | Cosmology and astronomy | Contains four trails: proofs of the creation of the world, the structure of the spheres and the stars, the seven climes of the earth, astronomy (tekhunah), and cosmic events such as solar and lunar eclipses [cite: 5, 7].
The Third Path | The creation of man and the laws of marital relations | Contains two trails: the creation of Adam and Eve, relations between the sexes, the laws of niddah, mikveh and immersion, and the spiritual and physiological aspects of procreation [cite: 5, 7].
The Fourth Path | Embryology, anatomy and pathology | Contains three trails: the development of the fetus in the womb, the structure of the organs of the human body, the physiology of the body's systems, and the functioning of the kidneys and the liver [cite: 5, 7, 11].
The Fifth Path | The regimen of bodily health and nutrition | Divided in two: Part 1 (10 trails) deals with hygiene and preventive medicine. Part 2 includes an alphabetical dictionary of foods, their properties and their clinical and health effects [cite: 7, 12].
The Sixth Path | The science of the soul and the intellect | Contains one trail: the essence of the soul, its faculties, the division of the soul into three parts (rational, irascible, appetitive), and ten fundamental questions about the intellect and the soul [cite: 5, 7, 12].
The Seventh Path | The health of the soul and ethics | Contains one trail: the correction of character traits, mental hygiene, and the spiritual elevation attained through the fulfillment of the commandments of the Torah [cite: 5, 7].
The Eighth Path | Faith in the Oral Torah and the aggadah | Contains one trail: the authority of the sages, the grounding of the tradition of the Oral Torah, and the explanation of the aggadot of the Sages that seem naive by way of allegory and secret [cite: 5, 7].
The Ninth Path | Reward, punishment and transmigration of souls | Contains one trail: reward and punishment, a description of the Garden of Eden and Gehinnom, the survival of the soul after death, and the doctrine of the transmigration of souls [cite: 5, 7, 13].
The Tenth Path | Faith in the redemption and the resurrection of the dead | Contains one trail: the vision of the future redemption, the coming of the Messiah, the order of the resurrection of the dead (the luz bone), and eternal existence in the World to Come [cite: 5, 7, 14, 15].
Epistemology and Intellectual Synthesis: Kabbalah, Philosophy and the Natural Sciences
The scholarly and intellectual teaching of Rabbi Meir ibn Aldabi is characterized by a consolidating attempt to bridge different conceptual worlds: Aristotelian and Maimonidean philosophical rationalism on the one hand, and the mystical wisdom of the school of the Ramban and the book of the Zohar on the other [cite: 2, 5].
Rabbi Meir is not a speculative kabbalist working in isolation from scientific inquiry; he has great respect for the natural sciences and for logic, but sets clear limits to them [cite: 2, 5]. Whereas rational inquiry serves as an essential tool for understanding the physics, cosmology and anatomy of the created world, in the profound metaphysical questions, such as the essence of the Godhead, the reasons for the commandments and eternal reward, the Kabbalah is the exclusive source of pure truth [cite: 2, 5].
The Theory of the Hebrew Origin of the Sciences
In order to resolve the perceived contradiction between the scientific disciplines being the heritage of the sages of Greece and of the nations and the sanctity of Torah wisdom, Aldabi adopted a historiographical theory that was widespread among Jewish thinkers in the Middle Ages [cite: 5, 16]. According to this view, the sole origin of all the natural sciences, astronomy and philosophy lies not in Greece but in the wisdom of King Solomon, in the sages of the Sanhedrin and in the exile of Jehoiachin in Jerusalem [cite: 5, 16].
Aldabi unfolds a narrative according to which, when Jerusalem was conquered by Alexander the Great, his teacher Aristotle was placed in charge of King Solomon's treasury of books [cite: 16]. Aristotle copied the scientific and natural sciences from Solomon's writings, appropriated them for himself and published them under his own name [cite: 16]. To disguise his theft and not reveal the Hebrew origin of the writings, Aristotle inserted into his writings grave errors and corrupt views, such as the claim that the world is eternal and the denial of individual providence [cite: 5, 16]. By means of this theory Aldabi justified the study of the natural sciences and of Greek philosophy, while purifying the material of the Aristotelian corruptions and returning it to its kabbalistic and Torah sources [cite: 5, 16].
Physiology, Anatomy and the Doctrine of Health
The medical chapters of "Shevilei Emunah" (the fourth and fifth Paths) were widely circulated and became a practical and medical guide for the educated public for generations [cite: 4, 5, 11]. Aldabi displays great expertise in the theory of the four humors of Hippocrates and Galen, and combined it with the conclusions of Arab physicians such as Ibn Rushd (Averroes) [cite: 11, 12].
His physiological conception bases the vitality of the body on the balance of the "natural heat" residing in the heart, which breathing and proper nutrition are meant to regulate and cool [cite: 12]. He offers an anatomical and spiritual analysis of the organs of the body, such as the kidneys, which serve not only as a physiological organ of excretion but also as the source of a person's counsel and hidden thought, as explained in the sayings of the Sages and in Scripture [cite: 11]. In his work this analysis is connected directly to halakhic ruling in the laws of terefot and the kashrut of animals [cite: 11].
The Sources of the Work, Textual Analysis and the Scholarly Controversy
In modern scholarship "Shevilei Emunah" is examined as an eclectic work combining diverse sources [cite: 5, 6, 7]. The central and most prominent source from which Aldabi borrowed entire chapters, sometimes editing and abridging them, is the encyclopedic work "Sha'ar ha-Shamayim" ("Gate of Heaven"), composed by the sage R. Gershom ben Shlomo of Narbonne (late 13th century) [cite: 2, 5].
Further sources incorporated in the work include:
The book "Olam ha-Katan" ("The Microcosm") by Rabbi Yosef ibn Tzaddik [cite: 5].
The book "Tagmulei ha-Nefesh" ("The Rewards of the Soul") by Rabbi Hillel ben Shmuel of Verona [cite: 5].
The writings of the Rambam (the Guide of the Perplexed, Hilkhot Yesodei ha-Torah, and medical treatises).
The commentaries of the Ramban on the Torah and the book of the Zohar [cite: 2].
The responsa of the Rashba (in particular on the explanation of the aggadot of the Sages in the eighth Path) [cite: 5].
The Scholarly Controversy over His Method of Editing
In the 19th century, with the beginnings of the Science of Judaism (Wissenschaft des Judentums), a stormy debate arose over the character of Aldabi's writing [cite: 2]. The scholar Nehemiah Brüll (1874) accused Aldabi of plagiarism and of undeclared use of texts from "Sha'ar ha-Shamayim" by Gershom ben Shlomo [cite: 2].
Against him, the eminent bibliographer Moritz Steinschneider came to Aldabi's defense [cite: 2]. Steinschneider argued that this accusation was anachronistic; in medieval literature the editing, anthologizing and reworking of earlier texts were considered a valued and legitimate literary craft, intended to make complex wisdom accessible to the broad public [cite: 2]. Aldabi did not seek to adorn himself with borrowed feathers, but to create a comprehensive guidebook combining science and faith [cite: 2, 5]. Later studies, conducted by Prof. Dov Schwartz and Prof. Resianne Fontaine, showed how Aldabi is not a passive copyist but an active editor who reworks, trims and integrates his sources within the defined theological-kabbalistic structure he designed [cite: 17, 18, 19].
Printing History, Reception and Influence in Later Generations
"Shevilei Emunah" enjoyed an exceptional reception and wide circulation in the Jewish world [cite: 4, 5]. For hundreds of years the work served as one of the main channels through which Torah students and scholars in Europe and in the lands of Islam were exposed to scientific, anatomical and cosmological knowledge [cite: 4, 5].
The prominent historical printings of the work attest to its continued circulation [cite: 3, 14, 20, 21, 22]:
Year of printing | Place of printing | Printer / distinctive features
5319 (1558–1559) | Riva di Trento | First edition (editio princeps). Printed by the physician Jacob Marcaria under the patronage of the papacy. Includes astronomical diagrams [cite: 4, 7, 20, 23, 24].
5387 (1627) | Amsterdam | Second edition. Printed at the press of Daniel de Fonseca. One of the first Hebrew books printed in Amsterdam. Included in the libraries of the sages of the Portuguese community [cite: 14, 21, 22].
5467–5468 (1707–1708) | Amsterdam | Printed by Shlomo Proops in a small format. Includes glosses and an acrostic poem [cite: 8, 10, 25].
5578 (1818) | Vilna | An Eastern European edition that spread the book in the study halls of Lithuania and Poland [cite: 3].
The Influence on Jewish Thought and Hasidism
The influence of the work is evident in the Torah and Hasidic literature of the 17th and 18th centuries [cite: 26, 27]:
The book Shnei Luchot ha-Brit (the holy Shelah): Rabbi Yeshayahu ha-Levi Horowitz quotes "Shevilei Emunah" extensively (in particular from the sixth and seventh Paths) as a basis for understanding the faculties of the soul, the holiness of marital union, and the spiritual refinement of the body [cite: 26, 27].
The Baal Shem Tov and the Hasidic movement: the book "Tzava'at ha-Rivash" contains a central passage in the name of the Baal Shem Tov explaining the verse "A righteous man knows the soul of his beast" (Proverbs 12:10) [cite: 26, 27]. The Hasidic explanation is based directly on the words of Rabbi Meir ibn Aldabi in the sixth Path, according to which the task of the righteous man is not to break materiality and the animal soul, but to connect it and refine it toward the service of the Creator [cite: 26, 27].
Conclusions
The scholarly-scientific work of Rabbi Meir ibn Aldabi, as reflected in his book "Shevilei Emunah", constitutes a unique historical and intellectual bridge in the history of Jewish thought [cite: 1, 3, 4, 5]. The grandson of the Rosh, raised on the knees of the pure halakhic tradition, succeeded in creating an encyclopedic work that unites science, anatomy and philosophy with the foundations of the Kabbalah and of faith [cite: 1, 2, 4, 5].
Through the ten structured Paths, Aldabi gave the Hebrew reader access to the whole range of fields of knowledge, from astronomy to reward and the soul, while conceiving of physical reality as a reflection of the divine order [cite: 2, 4, 5, 7]. His legacy continued to resonate for hundreds of years after his death in Jerusalem, and left a lasting mark on halakhic literature, Hasidic thought and the history of Hebrew science [cite: 1, 4, 5, 26, 27].
